issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette: Lily, a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian woman, has been married for nearly two decades and works as a Project Manager in a bustling tech company. Her life took an unexpected turn when she was diagnosed with a severe illness that nearly took her life. The trauma of the experience has left lasting psychological scars that continue to affect her daily functioning. Lily vividly remembers the hospital room, the smell of antiseptic, and the cold temperature that seemed to seep into her bones during those long days of treatment. These triggers are often activated by related smells, cold temperatures, or visual cues like medical equipment, which immediately transport her back to a place she desperately tries to escape. Every time Lily encounters these triggers at work-such as when a colleague opens a bottle of hand sanitizer, or the air conditioning is turned up too high-the memories flood back with overwhelming intensity. This has led her to adopt maladaptive strategies like attempting to erase the memory of the event and constantly monitoring her thoughts for signs of going crazy. The fear that she might not be in control of her mind becomes particularly acute when triggered. These triggers also influence how Lily remembers the traumatic event itself. She experiences a fragmented recollection where some moments are crystal clear while others remain completely blank. Additionally, there are times when she feels the full emotional intensity of the experience without any clear image or memory to accompany it. The extreme nature of these memories makes them difficult to reconcile with her current life, leaving her feeling as though they are almost too unreal to have happened. The negative appraisals that Lily holds about herself and her situation further exacerbate her suffering. She feels that her life has been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma, a belief that is reinforced by the fragmented nature of her memories and the intensity of her emotional responses. The idea that she has failed in her most important role in life adds to her sense of inadequacy and despair. This deep-seated belief that her body has been permanently damaged by what happened makes her acutely aware of any physical sensations, which can be triggered by even the smallest reminders. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies is evident in how Lily behaves at work. She avoids going near the medical equipment used for health screenings and tries to avoid cold rooms or spaces with strong smells that remind her of the hospital. This avoidance has led to a noticeable decline in her interactions with colleagues and her overall job performance, as she frequently misses important meetings or finds herself unable to focus. The maladaptive strategies Lily employs further reinforce her negative appraisals. Her attempts to erase memories often lead to increased anxiety when fragments resurface unexpectedly, confirming her fear that she is losing control of her mind. This, in turn, fuels the belief that her life has been irrevocably damaged and that she will never be able to reclaim her former sense of self. What finally brought Lily to seek help was a realization that these coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable. She could no longer ignore the impact her symptoms were having on her work and relationships. The memory of being unable to fully control herself during moments of intense emotional recall, coupled with her fear of never regaining the life she once had, drove her to reach out for support. Lily is most afraid that the trauma will define her forever, leaving her trapped in a cycle of avoidance and negative self-perception. She hopes that through therapy, she can regain some control over her memories and fears, ultimately finding a way to integrate these experiences into her life without them consuming her entirely.
